questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: My personal development, to meet people from other countries and to improve my english skills, to try different methods of learning than at my home university

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The possibilities to build a social life in the host country (possibilities for joining societies, for sharing accommodation with others, etc.).

That I was able to speak the language (english), so that it was easier for me to "get around"

The courses available - that there were at least some of them I found interesting

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of information available, but it was a bit difficult to keep track of everything, because there was actually so much information. But it was definitely possible to figure out.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I collected my key to my accommodation at the reception and was directed to my house.

We had gotten some e-mails about different social events in the beginning of terms (both in person and online) which I attended, but otherwise I was pretty much "left to myself", and had to go out and meet people etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
There were different colleges that you could live in. You could see the different ones available on the university web-page and make a prioritized list.
All 1st-year students (including exchange-students) were guaranteed a room on campus (for one year max).

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
In my house we had a shared kitchen (for 12 people), with two ovens, two sinks etc.
There were also options available on campus to buy food in the different restaurants on campus (a deal where you have a certain amount of money everyday that you had to spent on one meal), but I didn't choose this option. I cooked my self in the kitchen in my house.
If you live in a house with no kitchen (or only a small one) there were some catered or part-catered options, I think.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I think it is important to note that there is a lot of people who are 1st-year students who live on campus - this is because every 1st year student is guaranteed to live on campus for the 1st year. Afterwards, students go to live in the city and rent a house or an apartment.
My experience was that the people living on campus in my house (and everywhere else) was a lot younger than me (18-19 years old). This is not necessarily negative, and for some it worked fine.
But for at lot of the exchange-students, we could sometimes feel the age-difference, since we were all 3rd year students or post-graduate students. In "Darwin Houses" there were almost only exchange students who were a little older.
This is good to know, I think. Otherwise it is great to live on campus, since most of the social stuff is going on there and you live close by when going to class, on the library etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The course registration process was a bit frustrating because we were told VERY late in the process which courses we could choose between, and we had not been told that we were supposed to wait to find courses available. 
So I looked at courses from the very beginning, and in the end I could only choose between maybe 12 courses out of all of them. So I had spent a lot of time choosing courses I was very exited about only to find out that they weren't available for exchange students that are only here for one term.
Once the courses available were published, the process of choosing them was very easy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I could write on e-mail to the host university's "Erasmus-employees", and they could help me most of the time.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: There was only one of the courses that I finally chose that was not available/already full out of 4. I could choose another one instead.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I would advice you to ask the host university early on in the process, which courses will be available for just you (as an exchange student staying for maybe only one term), since this puts some restrictions on which courses you can choose between.
Remember also to look at which term (autumn or spring) the course is available in, and for how long the course is taking place (some take place over both terms, which might make it impossible for you to choose it).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses was the same as in Copenhagen, but because of the different teaching style there were other expectations of you.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching was different from that of UCPH.
The classes were only 50 minutes long, so there wasn't much teaching. I think it was a bit short for class discussions etc. And the seminars were a lot of talking very briefly about the subject - not a review of the syllabus as we (often) do in Denmark. There were always a "seminar sheet" which you had to prepare for class containing some questions to discuss in class. But otherwise it was very brief (since there was also only 50 minutes).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Environmental Law
Critical and Legal Reasoning
Privacy, Data Protection and Cybersecurity Law
Law and International Development

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend the course "Privacy, Data Protection and Cybersecurity Law" - a really cool course that surprised me a lot. The topics were really interesting and had a lot of ethical dilemmas to discuss in class.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You had to buy plates, cutlery, pans, pots etc. in the beginning, since the house was empty

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It was almost the same as in Denmark, maybe a little cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There was a lot of societies you could join. There was singing, dancing, sports, academic interests etc. 
There were "global hangouts" for people from different cultures to meet each other.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend joining any society - they do social stuff each week and there is a lot of people who study different things than yourself, and you find both exchange students and local students there.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to some of the cities around Canterbury (Dover, Whitstable etc.) or to London or Cambridge which is also close by (1-2 hours away).
Go to the city or to the woods nearby campus for a walk.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was okay. But there are differences between England and Denmark, of course.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Live with other students, join societies (!), join different groups on social media for exchange students or other groups of people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not anything really challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of parties and people were very social and a lot of fun.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be open to getting to know people, join all the social events you can manage.
Try not to have any specific expectations because things will often be different than exactly how you imagined it.
Ask all the questions you need - there is a lot of help to get both from students who already know the place when you get there and from the administration and student-help.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Canterbury is not a big city. But on the other hand, you get to live on campus and experience that.
University of Kent is very multinational and there are people from really all around the world (both taking their whole degree or being there as exchange students), which I think was really great to experience.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Of course the social part - you meet people from all around the world and spent a lot of time with them and go to parties and on trips etc.
I have become much more confident in speaking in English.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
It is always a bit challenging to go to a new country, live in a new place, study in a different language etc. all at once and without any family/friends from home nearby - it is possible to get a feeling that it is all a bit much/overwhelming.

I also had some challenges understanding the way the exams/assessments work because it was different from the exams I have taken in Denmark. But as time went, I understood more and more what was expected of me. But it was difficult some of the time, I think.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
